summary:
SPHEREx Blink is an interactive astronomical data visualisation platform designed to help users explore and understand moving objects in space using real images from NASA's SPHEREx mission. It addresses the challenge of making complex astronomical data easier to access, interpret and analyse.

The platform allows users to browse different observations of the same region of the sky frame by frame. By comparing images taken at different times, users can identify objects that move or change in brightness. It also provides tools to inspect individual pixels, view spectra, track brightness over time and identify stars using Gaia DR3 data.
details:
How does it work?

Users can enter Right Ascension and Declination coordinates to explore specific sky regions. They can:

  • Play, pause and adjust the speed of astronomical observations.
  • Compare normal, difference and stacked image displays.
  • Change wavelength detector bands and colour settings.
  • Inspect individual pixels to view their spectrum and brightness over time.
  • Identify stars using Gaia DR3 data.

What are its benefits and intended impact?

SPHEREx Blink makes astronomical observations more interactive and understandable. It helps students, astronomy enthusiasts and researchers explore real scientific data, recognise moving objects and investigate changes in celestial brightness. Its intended impact is to make space exploration and scientific discovery more accessible.

What technologies were used?

  • HTML: Website structure.
  • CSS: Styling, responsive layouts and light/dark themes.
  • JavaScript: Interactive controls, image processing and data visualisation.
  • Python: Backend server for retrieving and processing astronomical data.
  • JSON: Storing and transferring astronomical observations.
  • NASA/IPAC IRSA: SPHEREx astronomical data.
  • Gaia DR3: Star catalogue and proper-motion information.

How is the project creative?

The project transforms astronomical observations into an interactive visual experience. Instead of simply displaying static space images, it allows users to watch observations frame by frame, compare differences and investigate individual pixels through scientific graphs.

What factors did the team consider?

We considered:

  • Accessibility: Making complex astronomical information easier to understand.
  • User experience: Providing simple controls and clear visualisations.
  • Accuracy: Using authentic astronomical datasets.
  • Performance: Optimising image loading and caching repeated requests.
  • Compatibility: Supporting different screen sizes and light/dark themes.
  • Educational value: Encouraging curiosity and interest in astronomy.
